title: Canada Faces Recession Risk as Trade War With US Threatens 100,000 Jobs
excerpt: Economists warn that a collapse of the USMCA free trade agreement could push Canada onto a 'permanently lower path,' with the auto sector bracing for 50 percent tariffs starting in 2027.
body:
• Trade consultants project upwards of 100,000 Canadian jobs could be lost if US tariffs remain, with manufacturers in Quebec, Ontario, and British Columbia most exposed
  • A collapse of the USMCA free trade agreement would push Canada into recession and onto a "permanently lower path," according to Oxford Economics
  • Trump's threatened 50 percent auto tariffs starting January 2027 could disproportionately hurt Midwestern US states dependent on Canadian-made components
  • Internal Canadian political divisions are emerging, with Ontario pushing aggressive retaliation while Alberta and Saskatchewan resist restricting energy exports

The escalating trade war between the United States and Canada is raising the specter of recession north of the border, with economists warning that tit-for-tat tariffs could cost more than 100,000 Canadian jobs and fundamentally alter the cross-border economic relationship.

After Washington imposed 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods last weekend, Prime Minister Mark Carney on Tuesday unveiled retaliatory measures against more than 700 US products, also valued at $20 billion. Canada's tariffs, tiered at 15, 25, and 50 percent, are set to take effect on September 8, according to Al Jazeera.

Economic Fallout and Job Losses

While the tariffs will have a limited impact on the overall Canadian economy — Oxford Economics estimates they will shave 0.3 percentage points off gross domestic product next year — the damage will fall unevenly across provinces and sectors.

Manufacturers in Quebec, New Brunswick, and Ontario face the steepest losses, along with exporters in British Columbia, because they produce goods that are easily substitutable, according to Oxford Economics. Those include cement, paper, wood, beverages, clothing, plastics, and electronics.

"This absolutely is a trade war. We are feeling the effects in Canada and expect upwards of 100,000 jobs to be lost."

— Ashley Kalyn, International Trade Consultant, Peacock Tariff Consulting

Kalyn told Al Jazeera that her firm has already heard from clients planning to shut down factories and lay off workers if the tariffs remain in place.

USMCA Collapse Would Trigger Recession

Economists warn that a further deterioration in relations could end the free trade agreement between the United States, Mexico, and Canada, known as the USMCA. The agreement currently shields the majority of Canadian exports from US tariffs, keeping the effective tariff rate at 5.1 percent — among the lowest globally.

Even with the tariffs that took effect last weekend, the effective rate is estimated to rise to only 6.9 percent. But a full collapse of the USMCA would be far more damaging.

"That scenario would push Canada's economy into a recession and leave it on a permanently lower path," Tony Stillo, director of Canada Economics at Oxford Economics, warned in a note shared with Al Jazeera.

Auto Industry Braces for 50 Percent Tariffs

Trump's threat to double automobile tariffs to 50 percent starting in January 2027 has rattled the cross-border car industry. The existing 25 percent tariffs on cars and car parts, imposed early in Trump's second term with an exemption for USMCA-compliant parts, had been largely absorbed by manufacturers and dealerships.

But the proposed doubling would overwhelm those buffers. Bernard Yaros, lead US economist at Oxford Economics, said the auto industry's ability to absorb costs is "wearing thin" and that the 50 percent tariffs would "disproportionately hurt" Midwestern states such as Michigan, Ohio, and Indiana whose auto sectors depend on Canadian-made components.

The timing is significant: the tariff increase would arrive months after US midterm elections, leaving Trump "less fettered" by domestic politics and potentially setting "the stage for a more volatile tariff environment during the final two years of Trump's second term," Yaros said, according to Al Jazeera.

Political Divides Within Canada

The trade war is also exposing internal rifts. Ontario Premier Doug Ford has advocated a hardline approach, warning that "everything is on the table" in terms of retaliation, including cutting off electricity and critical mineral exports to the United States. But Alberta and Saskatchewan have declined to embrace such tactics, rejecting proposals to add export taxes to oil and potash — major economic pillars of their provinces.

"A war of attrition will help neither economy. But Canada is showing itself to be very resilient."

— Matthew Holmes, Executive Vice President, Canadian Chamber of Commerce

Vina Nadjibulla, cofounder and CEO of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, said the world is watching how Canada handles its increasingly hostile neighbor. "Whether Canada is able to hold this line has implications for others as well," she said.

The key date is September 8, when Canada's reciprocal tariffs take effect. "It's really hard to predict where this goes," Nadjibulla said. "The mood this week is about escalation."
